question: What is the main job of the systemic circulation in our body?

options.A: Delivering oxygenated blood to body tissues
options.B: Pumping blood directly into the alveoli
options.C: Filtering waste products inside the kidneys
options.D: Producing red blood cells in bone marrow

explanation: You've got this! Think of systemic circulation as the body's delivery service, carrying fresh oxygen and nutrients from the left side of the heart out to all your organs and tissues. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the rest of the body?
explanation: Great job! The left ventricle is the heavy lifter with thick muscles designed to push blood through the entire body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h1)

question: Through which valve does blood flow as it leaves the left ventricle?
explanation: Spot on! The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle directly into the aorta. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: Why is the muscular wall of the left ventricle much thicker than the right ventricle?

options.A: To prevent backflow into the upper respiratory tract
options.B: To store extra blood volume during periods of rest
options.C: To pump blood through the high-resistance systemic circuit
options.D: To handle blood returning directly from the pulmonary veins

explanation: Think about it: pumping blood to just the lungs is a short trip, but pushing it through your entire body takes a lot of pressure and muscle power! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which blood vessels act as the main controllers of blood flow resistance in the body?
explanation: Arterioles are like the adjustable taps of the circulatory system. Their muscular walls change size to control how much blood flows into the tiny capillaries. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: What happens when the smooth muscle in an arteriole contracts and narrows the vessel?

options.C: Venous return increases without any resistance
options.D: Vasoconstriction decreases blood flow to tissues

explanation: When vessels tighten up (vasoconstriction), less blood gets through to that area. Makes total sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h3)

question: How does oxygen mainly move across the tiny walls of a capillary into your cells?
explanation: Oxygen naturally likes to move from crowded areas (high concentration in the blood) to less crowded areas (tissue cells) without needing extra energy. That's diffusion! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: What main force pushes fluid out of the capillaries and into the tissues?
explanation: Think of hydrostatic pressure simply as the pushing pressure of blood inside the vessel, forcing plasma and nutrients out through the capillary walls. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: What structures inside your veins stop blood from flowing backward?
explanation: Spot on! Venous valves act like little one-way doors, helping push blood all the way back up to the heart against gravity. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why is blood pressure so much lower in the veins compared to the arteries?

options.A: Veins have much thicker walls to absorb pressure
options.B: Gravity completely eliminates pressure in lower extremities
options.C: The right atrium actively pulls blood out of the veins
options.D: Friction through capillary beds causes a major pressure drop

explanation: As blood squeezes through miles of tiny, narrow capillaries, it loses a lot of energy to friction, so by the time it reaches the veins, the pressure has dropped a lot. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which of these has the quickest and biggest effect on blood flow resistance?
explanation: Even a tiny change in the width (radius) of a blood vessel makes a huge difference in how hard it is for blood to flow through! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h6)

question: If a patient's blood vessels suddenly narrow severely (vasoconstriction), what happens to their total resistance?
explanation: You've got this! Narrower pipes mean more resistance for the heart to pump against. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which clinical sign is a clear warning of poor blood flow to the body's outer parts (periphery)?
explanation: When you press a nail bed and it takes too long for the pink color to return, it tells you blood isn't flowing smoothly through the small vessels. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h7)

question: You check a patient's feet and notice their pulses are very weak and thready. What does this usually mean?

options.A: Excessive cardiac output from the left ventricle
options.B: High systemic blood pressure in large arteries
options.C: Severe vasodilation throughout the entire body
options.D: Reduced blood flow to the lower extremities

explanation: Weak pulses tell you there's not enough blood getting down to the feet. Always trust your assessment skills! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h7)

question: Why do patients with poor blood circulation often produce very little urine?

options.A: Peripheral veins absorb excess water before it reaches kidneys
options.B: Urine production stops because the liver stops filtering blood
options.C: The bladder actively retains fluid to increase blood pressure
options.D: Reduced blood flow to the kidneys lowers filtration pressure

explanation: Your kidneys need good blood pressure and flow to do their filtering job. If circulation drops, urine output drops too! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h8)

question: In an elderly patient, what is often the very first sign that the brain isn't getting enough blood flow?
explanation: The brain is super sensitive to oxygen drops. Any sudden confusion or change in alertness is an important red flag we watch out for in nursing! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h8)
